document.note: Section of Dean's oral history on his India service and his removal by the Reagan administration on grounds of mental instability. He traces his shift toward Gandhi's and the Soviet position on post-withdrawal Afghanistan and blames Reagan and Pakistan policy for supporting fundamentalists.

President Carter approved original intelligence funding for Afghan resistance.

Far Eastern Economic Review reports Andrew Eiva's Senate testimony alleging ISI theft of aid and that $700 million of $1.09 billion earmarked for Afghan rebels disappeared.

Bush, as vice president, made a bargain in Pakistan with men described as guardians of Pakistan's heroin kingdom.

Embassy New Delhi sends telegram (Message 0130) to the Department of State reporting the article on drugs and Pakistan.
Soviet invasion of Afghanistan.

Solarz writes to President Bush urging a cut-off of aid to Pakistan over its nuclear program (Pressler Amendment).
Dean flown to Switzerland for a roughly 6-week forced rest until end of October 1988.

Rajiv Gandhi writes a farewell letter to Ambassador Dean.

Dean meets Sonia Gandhi in New Delhi.
Rajiv Gandhi was assassinated.

Establishment of the U.S.-India Fund from $200 million PL 480 rupee funds for cooperation in education, science, technology and agriculture.
Indian Navy leased a Soviet nuclear submarine to train its crew.

Security breach at the American Consulate General in Madras; American employee expelled within 24 hours.
India refused to sign the Nuclear Proliferation Treaty as drafted.
Israeli Vice Consul in Bombay elevated to Consul General with jurisdiction extended to Cochin.

The Herald published eyewitness report of NLC trucks carrying heroin from NWFP to Karachi.
General Fazle Huq denied drug allegations in a Pakistan press interview.
Bhopal chemical disaster: toxic cloud from Union Carbide plant killed 16,000-30,000.

Dean wrote a paper comparing Indian and Pakistani nuclear programs (New Delhi telegram 29183 of Dec 3, 1987).
Rajiv Gandhi met Israeli Foreign Minister Peres at the UN in New York via private circles.
Caspar Weinberger visited India, first US Defense Secretary visit in many years.
M-1 Abrams tank demonstration at Bahawalpur attended by Zia, Raphel and Wassom.
Zia's C-130 (Pak One) crashed minutes after takeoff from Bahawalpur, killing all 31 aboard including Zia, Raphel and Wassom.
Ronen Sen told Dean a satellite may have filmed Zia's plane take off and crash.
Epstein's Vanity Fair article 'How General Zia went down' published, suggesting a gas bomb.
Kabul cables reporting Yegorychev's protests to Charge Glassman on alleged 'Hollywood production' of incursion reports.
Sundarji ordered Indian troops to Sri Lanka at request of the Sri Lankan president.
Sundarji died.
Sundarji and wife Vani dined at Dean's Paris apartment; Sundarji said 'You did it' regarding Zia's death.
M-1 Abrams tank demonstration at Bahawalpur, attended by Zia, Raphel and Wassom; the tank missed its target.
Zia's C-130 (Pak One) crashed minutes after takeoff from Bahawalpur, killing all 31 aboard including Zia, Raphel, Wassom and Pakistani generals.
Ronen Sen phoned Dean at 4:00 p.m. with news of the crash; CIA staff were uninformed.
Oakley met General Beg, discussed M-1 tank purchase and regional 'strategic consensus'.
Oakley reported on the Beg meeting in Islamabad cable No. 7535.
Report that CIA requested $55 million to buy back Stinger missiles given to Afghan rebels.

key_claims: Dean says US policy toward India was incoherent, with different departments pursuing conflicting policies and Washington sometimes bypassing the ambassador.
Rajiv Gandhi argued India's turn to Soviet arms was due to US refusal to supply spares and ammunition during the 1971 war, and was consistent with non-alignment.
Dean claims the Pentagon and intelligence agencies were favorably disposed toward Pakistan in 1985.
Dean says Pakistan had to import or obtain illegally the parts for its nuclear program, which he reported to Washington.
Dean persuaded Under Secretary Armacost to have a Senate committee resolution equating India and Pakistan on nuclear matters reversed.
The U.S. in the 1980s tended to equate India and Pakistan on nuclear issues, which Rajiv Gandhi resented.
Pentagon weapons supplied to Pakistan were sometimes destined for Afghan fighters, and Indian intelligence knew their final destination.
U.S. and India held different goals for Afghanistan: a pro-western Afghanistan versus non-alignment.
The role of the Pakistani Intelligence Service in Afghanistan clouded U.S.-India defense cooperation.
Overriding U.S. policy in South Asia was 'to trap and kill the Russian bear in Afghanistan' with Pakistan as staunch ally.
Dean links arms for Afghan fighters to a boom in the drug culture in Pakistan and Afghanistan.
The CIA weapons pipeline to the Afghan Mujahidin was run through Pakistan's ISI, using the Army-owned National Logistic Cell and PAF transports.
NLC trucks were allegedly used to carry heroin from NWFP to Karachi.
Almost all Afghan opium production was said to be controlled by Pakistan-based syndicates with links to liberated areas.
Zia-ul-Haq's adopted son Hamid Hasnain was arrested as a drug kingpin in 1984 while the US praised Zia on narcotics control.
Army and Air Force officers caught with heroin in 1986 escaped custody, suggesting syndicates within the Pakistan Army.
Andrew Eiva alleged ISI under Akhtar Abdul Rahman stole US aid funds ($700m of $1.09bn).
The CIA subordinated DEA investigations abroad and the US avoided pressing Pakistan for narcotics arrests.
Volunteer fighters were initially trained by US Green Berets and ISI under CIA management with funding from US, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia.
Veterans of the Afghan war later trained insurgents in Algeria, Egypt, Indonesia, Lebanon, Philippines, Tajikistan and Yemen.
Casey's October 1984 trip led to NSDD 166 in March 1985, escalating covert action including Stinger missiles.
The US covertly backed Hekmatyar, who received most arms and funds, until Massoud entered Kabul in April 1992.
Zia wanted a Kabul government closely linked to Islamabad, and the US sympathized more with Pakistan's vision than India's.
Dean suggests the US had overt and covert Afghan policies, the latter aimed at a pro-Pakistani, anti-communist government.
The US covertly backed Peshawar-based Afghan fundamentalists, with Hekmatyar described as 'our man'.
India sought a secular, balanced Kabul government and opposed exclusive Pakistani influence.
Pakistan's leadership, per Raphel, sought strategic depth through a friendly Afghanistan.
US assessments in 1988 wrongly discounted a fundamentalist takeover in Kabul.
Zia died on 17 Aug 1988 in a plane crash after attending an M-1 tank demonstration at Bahawalpur.
Gen. Beg claimed there would be no fundamentalist government in Afghanistan and envisioned a Pakistan-Afghanistan-Iran-Turkey consensus.
Dean argues Zia's death was an assassination followed by a cover-up, favouring Epstein's gas-bomb theory.
Dean believed US policy tilted toward Pakistan and supported fundamentalist Afghan resistance to take Kabul.
Stingers supplied to the Afghan resistance later became a terrorism risk, prompting CIA buy-back efforts in 1993.
Gen. Sundarji linked Zia's death to Afghanistan and suspected Mossad hostility to Pakistan, later suggesting US involvement.
Soviet ambassador Yegorychev claimed evidence of Soviet/Afghan incursions into Pakistan was manufactured by CIA or ISI.
Dean believed US policy in South Asia amounted to full support for the most fundamentalist Islamic movements to take over Kabul.
Dean said the US supplied $700 million annually to the Afghan resistance, per the NYT editorial.
The NYT editorial said guerrilla leaders doubled as drug kingpins and Peshawar became a by-word for corruption.
Dean speculated, without evidence, that pro-Israeli circles colluded with anti-Zia elements in the 17 Aug 1988 crash.
Dean claimed the State Department used medical questioning of his sanity to sideline him before the November 1988 US election.
